source: Xia et al. (2025) Live-SWE-agent: Can Software Engineering Agents Self-Evolve on the Fly?
finding: On current models a bash-only agent (mini-SWE-agent) is already strong. Letting the agent write its own small tools on top of bash adds a few points, not a leap. The gain is model dependent and negative for the weakest model.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified, % resolved, mini-SWE-agent vs Live-SWE-agent: GPT-5-Mini 59.8 vs 63.0 ($0.04 vs $0.05); GPT-5 65.0 vs 68.4; Claude 4.5 Sonnet 70.6 vs 75.4 ($0.56 vs $0.68); Gemini 3 Pro 74.2 vs 77.4. 50-problem ablation: no tool creation 62.0, tool creation without per-step reflection 64.0, with reflection 76.0; GPT-5-Nano 44.0 -> 14.0.
limits: Ablation is 50 problems, single run, so 2-4 point gaps are noise-level; only the 14-point reflection effect is large. Cost is similar but not token-equal.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the 2024 interface gain (11 to 18 on Lite) was against a weak shell baseline. In 2025 a plain shell gets 60-74%. A designed layer still adds 3-5 points on strong models; the per-step reminder to reconsider tools is the largest piece.

source: Du et al. (2025) Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval
finding: Even when the model retrieves the needed evidence perfectly, accuracy drops as input grows. The drop persists when the extra tokens are whitespace or masked out of attention, and when evidence sits right before the question.
numbers: 5 LLMs, math/QA/code tasks; drops of 13.9% to 85% as length grows within claimed limits; masked distraction: at least 7.9% drop at 30K masked tokens for both models tested. Recite-then-solve fix: Mistral-v0.3-7B synthetic GSM8K 70.6/49.3/43.4/41.6/35.5 baseline vs 76.2/71.4/66.7/69.1/66.7 at 0/3750/7500/15000/26250 tokens.
quote: the sheer length of the input alone can hurt LLM performance, independent of retrieval quality
limits: Biggest drops on open models; closed models drop less on some tasks. Fix tested on few models.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: length itself costs accuracy, so the code should keep shown state short and rebuild a compact prompt per step, not only reorder it. Recite-then-solve is a cheap code-side move.

source: Modarressi et al. (2025) NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching
finding: When the needle shares no words with the question, long-context scores fall steeply. Of 13 models claiming at least 128K, 11 fall below 50% of their short-context baseline at 32K.
numbers: GPT-4o 99.3 base, 98.1 (1K), 95.7 (4K), 89.2 (8K), 81.6 (16K), 69.7 (32K). Llama 3.3 70B 97.3 base, 42.7 at 32K. Claude 3.5 Sonnet 87.5 base, 29.8 at 32K. Gemini 1.5 Pro 92.6 base, 48.2 at 32K. GPT-4o mini 13.7 at 32K. Effective length (within 85% of base): GPT-4o 8K, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 4K, most others 1-2K.
limits: Tests latent-association retrieval, not code-laid-out state; 2024 to early 2025 models; no 2026 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: effective context is far shorter than claimed. Design for a few thousand tokens of state per step. Where checks and goals go is still not tested directly.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: 15 top LLMs do much worse when the instruction arrives in pieces over turns than when given whole. Most of the loss is unreliability, not lost ability. Models make early assumptions and do not recover. Restating all earlier information each turn recovers only part.
numbers: Average drop 39% across six generation tasks, 200,000+ simulated conversations; unreliability up 112% in multi-turn. Snowball (restate all prior shards each turn) recovers 15-20% of the FULL-to-SHARDED loss with GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini; Recap (one final restatement) does better but is unrealistic. Reasoning models (o3, DeepSeek-R1) deteriorate similarly; their answers are on average 33% longer. Temperature 0 does not fix multi-turn unreliability.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Tests underspecified user instructions, not rule constraints in an agent loop. Snowball tested on 4 tasks, 2 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: repeating prior content each turn helps only partly (15-20% recovery). The code should rebuild state from scratch each step instead of appending a long dialogue that carries early wrong assumptions.

source: Terminal coding agent technical report (2026) Building Effective AI Coding Agents for the Terminal: Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering
finding: A system report describes event-driven reminders injected at the decision point as user-role messages, with caps on how often each fires, to stop instruction fade-out in long sessions. It says user-role reminders gave noticeably higher compliance than system-role in early experiments. No quantitative table.
numbers: No compliance numbers given. Design facts: one-shot flags and attempt counters per reminder; reminders that fired every iteration made the agent loop on the nudge itself.
quote: Inject reminders at the point of decision, not upfront
limits: Engineering lessons, not a controlled experiment; author list not recorded.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: supports putting rules into each state's prompt at the moment they matter (Zhang and Norman analogue), with caps. It is a hypothesis for our A/B test, not evidence.

source: Yang et al. (2026) Agents' Overreliance on Unreliable Tools
finding: 14 models with web search, an LLM sub-agent and a code executor were given plausible but corrupted returns. They adopted the corrupted content often, even overriding correct no-tool answers. They questioned the return in their reasoning but rarely warned the user. A verification instruction helped most.
numbers: P1 corruption mean adoption: search 68.0%, sub-agent 40.1%, code executor 35.5%. P2 (unrelated or large numeric error): 12.6%, 27.3%, 24.5%. Override of answers right without tools: search 56.4%, sub-agent 26.8%, code executor 33.5%. QuALITY sub-agent adoption 94.7%, override 91.9%. Warnings to user in 4.2% of final answers (search and code). Verification prompts cut adoption on all three tools; Low/High reliability labels gave partial gains on search; post-training gave limited gains.
limits: Corruptions are injected; real tool error rates differ. Preprint (Sept 2026).
agent_relevance: Gap 5: models over-trust tools, and the code should not assume the model will check. Add a verification instruction and an independent code-side check at key steps; reliability labels help only partly.

source: Sun et al. (2024) Tools Fail: Detecting Silent Errors in Faulty Tools
finding: When a tool silently returns wrong output, small models overtrust it. A detect-and-reject step reaches 60-70 F1 on an accept/reject task for better models. Warnings and checklists help.
numbers: Accept/Reject F1 of 60-70 for the better models (Table 3, two tasks: calculator math and ALFRED).
limits: 2024 models; I read the text and the Table 3 summary, not every table.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: earlier support that silent tool errors are not caught by default; detection must be asked for.

source: Cheng, Pan, Amiri (2026) Investigating Tool-Memory Conflicts in Tool-Augmented LLMs
finding: Models' own answer and the tool's result disagree often. The disagreement lowers accuracy on math. Strong models split about evenly between trusting tool and memory. Prompting and RAG fixes did not resolve conflicts.
numbers: Conflict rate: GPT-4o 14.1%, DeepSeek-v3 15.3%, Llama-3.3 70B 15.5%, Qwen-2.5 72B 26.9%, QwQ 75.4%, Llama-3 8B 83.2%, Watt 8B 48.6%; mean 49.8% over 7 models. Math accuracy falls 4.5 points on average under conflict. Tool bias: Llama-3.3 70B 44.3% vs memory bias 40.2%; DeepSeek-v3 39.2% vs 41.3%. Small models show tool bias under 1%.
limits: Tools treated as ground truth, so it is a when-to-trust test, not an over-trust test.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 6: strong models do not defer fully to a correct tool; small models ignore tools. The interface should state tool reliability and verify a sample.

source: Qian et al. (2025) SMART: Self-Aware Agent for Tool Overuse Mitigation
finding: Models call tools for questions they could answer from memory, and the extra tool use sometimes causes wrong answers. Training an agent (SMARTAgent) to separate knowledge steps from tool steps cuts tool calls and raises accuracy.
numbers: Preliminary study: Llama tool overuse rate above 50%. SMARTAgent: tool use reduced 24%, performance up over 37% (abstract); 7B and 8B SMARTAgents beat GPT-4o on some domains (Time, Math).
limits: Training approach, not prompting; Llama and Mistral era; three in-domain task types; no prediction-plus-feedback loop like Ngai and Gilbert.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: models do not calibrate tool use by default. A prompt-only version (state what you know before calling) is untested here.

source: Shen et al. (2025) Thinking vs. Doing: Agents that Reason by Scaling Test-Time Interaction
finding: Letting a web agent act and re-check more (information from the environment) beat spending the same tokens on longer thinking or best-of-n. Repeated re-checking by prompt alone eventually hurts.
numbers: WebArena: prompting 'check again' after the agent decides to stop lifts success 23% to 28%; equal-compute budget forcing or best-of-n gains under 3%. Budget forcing plateaus near 0.26. TTI-trained 12B Gemma 3 improves over its base by 9% and 8% on two benchmarks.
limits: Check-again at the end is not probe-before-commit; web tasks only; RL gains are separate from the prompt effect.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: acting to get information beat extra thinking per token in a web task. No direct test of cheap probes in code tasks. Too many re-checks confuse the agent.

source: Lee, D'Antoni, Berg-Kirkpatrick (2026) The Format Tax
finding: Format requests in the prompt cause most of the accuracy loss, not constrained decoding. Reasoning first then reformatting in a second pass (or extended thinking) recovers most of it. Recent closed models show little or no tax.
numbers: 6 open-weight models, 144 cells: 76 significant, 72 in the tax direction, 4 credit; qwen3-8b -9.9 points average (17 of 24 cells), nemotron3-nano -4.3. Older API models -5.2 points average without grammar decoding, -8.0 with. claude-haiku-4.5, grok-4.1-fast, gpt-5.4-nano show near-zero or positive deltas.
limits: Two-turn approach costs extra tokens; not designed as a token-equal comparison; preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: on current strong closed models the format tax is near zero, so JSON actions are fairly safe there. For small or open models use reason-then-format.

source: Fan (2026) Capacity, Not Format: Rethinking Structured Reasoning Failures
finding: Format cost depends on spare capacity. Strong models absorb JSON; models near their limit lose a lot, partly from truncation and partly from competing demands. Even Opus 4.7 loses 5.3 points on AIME. Reasoning freely first then formatting recovers most.
numbers: Sonnet 4.6 MATH-Hard Level 5: 88.7 JSON vs 89.3 CoT. Haiku 4.5 -36.2 points (p<0.0001) at standard budget; 80.7% prose vs 52.5% JSON. GPT-4o-mini -28.0 points with extended budget. Opus 4.7 AIME 96.2 to 91.0. Delayed-structure recovers to 80-87% (3-run mean).
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the tax returns on hard tasks even for frontier models. Let the model reason in free text, then have the code ask for the structured action in a second short step.

finding: JSON-schema constrained decoding with a reasoning field before the answer did not hurt and slightly helped a small model. This conflicts with the Tam et al. drop and suggests that a reasoning field placed first in the schema avoids the tax.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, LM-only vs Guidance: Last Letter 50.7 vs 54.0; Shuffle Objects 52.6 vs 55.9; GSM8K 80.1 vs 83.8. Up to 4% gain overall.
limits: One 8B model; schema held a reasoning field (not answer-only JSON); not token-equal.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: format harm depends on schema design. Keep a free reasoning field first.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) The Double Measurement Confound in Agent Benchmarks: De-Scaffolding
finding: When a fixed scaffold makes all execution-critical decisions, the score no longer measures the model. A rule-based script with no LLM scores close to the best LLMs, and two unrelated open models get byte-identical per-seed scores.
numbers: Mean scores about 97.5 for top configurations; rule-based script 96.8 (abstract text).
limits: A benchmark-validity paper on one pipeline; only the abstract and opening read closely.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 9: a scaffold can carry the whole result, so our benchmark must compare model-plus-scaffold with a bare model at equal tokens and include a control showing the scaffold alone does not solve the item.

source: Thangarajah, Chen, Hassan (2026) DCAS: Decoupling CLI Agent Scaffolding to Internalize Planning across Scaffolds
finding: Models fine-tuned under one scaffold (OpenHands) lose a lot under other scaffolds; untrained base models do not. A plan from a stronger model gives a big gain with the executor unchanged. Fine-tuning on planning turns alone raised no-plan accuracy, meaning it installed implicit conventions.
numbers: SWE-Lego-Qwen3-32B 52.6% OpenHands to 44.2% Claude Code; Nebius-SWE-Rebench-30B 49.7% to 20.4% on mini-swe-agent. Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B with Sonnet 4.5 plan: +15.0 Pass@1 (self-plan +5.4, open planner +6.4). PlanOnly SFT: 42.8 base to 53.8 without any plan (+11.0).
limits: SWE-bench Verified only; training-based, not in-context. Silent on whether a prompted scaffold leaves any trace in an untouched model.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: for a frozen model (our case) removing the scaffold removes its effect; no carry-over is shown. Dependence on conventions is real in fine-tuned models and absent in untouched ones.

source: Li, Qiao, Gao (2026) Which Metadata Matters for LLM Tool Selection in MCP?
finding: Across 5 LLMs and 5 tasks, the parameter schema moves tool choice more than the name or description. Models prefer separate top-level parameters over grouped ones. When only one schema fits an explicit requirement all five models choose it despite position bias.
numbers: 367,174 MCP tools analysed; effects estimated with conditional logistic regression on position-balanced trials.
limits: Selection among overlapping tools, not number of tools shown; effect sizes not read in full (abstract and intro only).
agent_relevance: Gap 10: how each operator is described changes choice. Write operators with flat parameters and clear parameter descriptions.

source: Gaurav et al. (2025) Dynamic ReAct: Scalable Tool Selection for Large-Scale MCP Environments
finding: Search-and-load of tools on demand cut tool loading by up to 50% while keeping task accuracy. Context-enriched embeddings raised tool retrieval top-5 accuracy by 50% relative (baseline 40% top-5, 64% top-10).
numbers: Up to 50% fewer tools loaded; baseline text-embedding-3-large 40% top-5.
limits: Small engineering paper; no fixed-small-set arm at equal prompt size, so gap 10 is not settled.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: retrieval per state saves tokens; whether it beats a hand-picked fixed set per state is untested. With 8 operators and 10 states a fixed per-state set is likely enough.

source: Kirsh and Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Tetris players rotate zoids physically to see their shape instead of mentally rotating them. Physical rotation is far faster than mental rotation. Early rotation also exposes the hidden part of an emerging zoid sooner.
numbers: A zoid can be rotated 90 degrees in as few as 100 ms vs an estimated 800 to 1200 ms mentally (pilot, Shepard-Metzler-style task). Pilot had 3 Tetris players (intermediate, advanced, expert), 8 presentations of each zoid pair; reaction time rose with angle 0 to 180 degrees. Rotating an emerging zoid shows its full image 150 to 300 ms earlier; at medium speed a zoid drops one square every 150 ms.
limits: Pilot with 3 subjects; the 800-1200 ms figure is an estimate.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: confirms the Tetris numbers used in K25. Small pilot, so illustration only, not an effect size.

source: Larkin and Simon (1987); Norman (1991); Hutchins (1995) founding human papers (access attempt)
finding: Direct download of the Wiley text was blocked (403) and guessed free URLs returned 404. I did not read Larkin and Simon, Norman 1991 or Hutchins 1995 in full this run.
limits: Gap 7 stays open for these three.
agent_relevance: Do not cite new numbers from them; keep earlier opened lines only.
